difficulties.response: Contrast sentences that report association and causation, and connect this to what research designs can support.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain in writing the effect of a fall in consumer income on the market for a normal good, using a diagram.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the assumption of a normal good, shows a shift of the demand curve, explains the effects on price and quantity with ceteris paribus, and avoids normative comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the correct direction of change but confuses shift and movement along, or omits conditions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives a general opinion about recession without model-based reasoning.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional economics pathways, focus on basic model language and diagram description. In UG in-sessional work, link it to essay and exam answers. At PGT, the emphasis shifts to empirical claims, econometric reporting and the hedging of causal claims.
reviewNotes: ESP research on economics discourse (for example on the language of economics textbooks and articles) could support this topic further once suitable sources are verified for the bibliography.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) shows how professional genres such as promotional and business letters are shaped by communicative purpose and by the relationship between writer and reader, and Zhu (2004) found that business courses assign memos, letters, reports and similar tasks that mimic workplace writing. Teaching should therefore contrast these genres with the essay: the main point first, organisation for a decision-maker, and tone fitted to role relationships. Because company and school templates differ, learners should analyse the specific brief, template and exemplars.

activities.title: Essay to memo
learnerActions: Read a short academic answer to a business question
Identify the recommendation and the two strongest reasons
Rewrite the content as a memo to a named manager, with the recommendation in the first sentence, and compare tone across the class
activities.intendedInsight: The same content is reorganised and re-voiced when the reader changes from marker to decision-maker.
activities.rationale: Rewriting across genres highlights how purpose and reader shape structure, as genre analysis of professional writing predicts.

activities.title: Pitch in three minutes
learnerActions: Analyse a recorded or transcribed pitch for its stages (problem, solution, benefits, evidence, request)
Plan a three-minute pitch for a product or project from your module using the same stages
Deliver the pitch and receive peer feedback on clarity of the request and evidence
activities.intendedInsight: A pitch is a persuasive genre with a predictable structure that ends in a specific request.
activities.rationale: Move analysis of a model before production applies genre pedagogy to a spoken professional genre that business schools assess.

difficulties.pattern: Writing memos and briefing notes as essays, with background first and the recommendation in the last paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memos marked down for structure or for burying the main point.
difficulties.response: Contrast reader needs in each genre and practise front-loading. Do not suggest that the essay structure is wrong; it suits a different purpose.

difficulties.pattern: Being very indirect or very blunt with a senior reader in a simulated workplace task.
difficulties.revealedBy: Memos that are either heavily mitigated and unclear or directive in a way that suits a superior rather than a subordinate.
difficulties.response: Discuss the role relationship in the brief and model wording at different levels of directness. Treat expectations as local business conventions, not universal norms.

diagnostic.task: Give a 300-word essay paragraph on a business issue and ask for a 120-word memo to a line manager recommending action.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Opens with purpose and recommendation, gives concise reasons, closes with a next step, and uses a tone suitable for a manager.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Shortens the text but keeps the essay order or an unsuitable tone.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the paragraph without a clear recommendation or reader orientation.

guidance.contextNotes: UG business students meet these genres in modules on management and communication. PGT students, especially on MBA-type programmes, are often assessed through reports, pitches and briefing papers, and some will already know workplace conventions from experience that may differ from the school's expectations.
reviewNotes: 'Bottom line up front' ordering is a widely taught convention, but expectations vary across organisations and cultures; it is presented as typical for assessed business-school memos.

guidance.summary: Management frameworks are useful prompts, but Hill and Westbrook (1997), studying SWOT use in companies, found that outputs tended to be long, unprioritised lists that were rarely used in later strategy work. That is the same pattern markers criticise in student work. Teaching should frame each framework as a means to an analytic end: select, evidence, prioritise and draw implications. Nathan (2013) shows that the analysis stage of the business case report is where such frameworks are expected to do this work.

activities.title: From list to analysis
learnerActions: Take an unprioritised SWOT or PESTLE table for a familiar company
Delete factors that lack evidence and rank the remainder by likely impact
Write a paragraph on the two most significant factors, explaining their implications and how internal and external factors interact
activities.intendedInsight: A framework produces analysis only when its contents are evidenced, prioritised and connected to a decision.
activities.rationale: Hill and Westbrook's finding that SWOT outputs are rarely prioritised or used shows why the move from list to implication is the teaching target.

activities.title: Choosing the right tool
learnerActions: Read three short case questions (for example entering a new market, improving internal efficiency, responding to a new competitor)
Decide which framework fits each question best and why
Write one sentence for each acknowledging what the chosen framework cannot capture
activities.intendedInsight: Frameworks answer different questions, and choosing one is itself an analytical decision with limitations.
activities.rationale: Justifying framework choice and limits reflects the evaluative use of frameworks expected in the analysis stage of case reports.

difficulties.pattern: Including every framework taught in the module to show knowledge.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports with several framework tables but little analysis, and feedback such as 'descriptive' or 'lacks depth'.
difficulties.response: Show markers' criteria and high-scoring exemplars that use one or two frameworks in depth. Discuss depth versus breadth.

difficulties.pattern: Listing factors as bullet points without evidence or implications.
difficulties.revealedBy: Framework tables with generic entries that could apply to any company.
difficulties.response: Require each factor to have a piece of evidence from the case and a 'so what' sentence. Avoid simply asking for more factors.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 150-word PESTLE-based paragraph on one external factor affecting a company described in a short case.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Selects a significant factor, supports it with case evidence and explains its implication for the company's decision.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a relevant factor but gives generic evidence or no implication.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists several PESTLE categories with one-line entries and no analysis.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional business pathways should introduce the analytical use of frameworks early. UG students meet many frameworks across modules. PGT students may have used frameworks at work and need to adjust to academic expectations of critique and evidence.

guidance.summary: Sackett et al. (1996) define evidence-based medicine as combining best current research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values, and explicitly reject the caricature of it as 'cookbook' practice. Health students often meet the concept through evidence hierarchies alone, so teaching should restore all three components and show how they surface in assignment language. Greenhalgh (2019) provides an accessible account of question framing and appraisal, and Gigerenzer et al. (2007) show why understanding how risk is expressed is part of using evidence well.

activities.title: Three-way decision
learnerActions: Read a short scenario in which research, clinical experience and patient preference point in different directions
In groups, list what each source of evidence contributes and what its limits are
Write a recommendation paragraph that integrates all three and compare it with a model written by a clinical lecturer
activities.intendedInsight: Evidence-based practice is a judgement that integrates research, expertise and patient values, and writing must show that integration.
activities.rationale: Working from Sackett et al.'s definition counters the narrower reading of evidence-based practice as following the highest-ranked study, and makes the expected argument structure explicit.

activities.title: From scenario to question
learnerActions: Read three brief clinical scenarios
Identify population, intervention, comparison and outcome for each and write a focused question
Turn each question into search terms and discuss which study design would best answer it
activities.intendedInsight: The type of question determines the type of evidence needed, which is one limitation of a single hierarchy.
activities.rationale: Question framing is the first step in evidence-based practice as described in the clinical literature, and linking question type to design addresses the over-reliance on one hierarchy.

difficulties.pattern: Evidence-based means the strongest study wins. If there is an RCT, that settles it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments that recommend interventions solely on the basis of trial results, with no discussion of context or patient perspective.
difficulties.response: Return to the three components and to examples where patient values or context change the decision. Show markers' comments that reward integration.

difficulties.pattern: Citing guidelines and textbooks as if they were primary evidence, or citing a source because it is authoritative rather than because of its evidence base.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reference lists dominated by textbooks and policy documents in assignments that ask for research evidence.
difficulties.response: Show the difference between a guideline, the studies it synthesises, and a textbook summary, and agree with subject staff what each assignment expects. Avoid framing the learner's earlier practice as wrong; treat it as a different convention.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain, in about 100 words, what evidence-based practice means and to give one example of when the best research evidence might not determine a decision.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names research evidence, clinical expertise and patient values and gives a plausible example where values or context shift the decision.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Defines it as using research evidence and mentions patients only in passing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates it with using any published source or with following guidelines.

guidance.contextNotes: On foundation programmes leading to health degrees, introduce the concept and PICO question framing. In UG in-sessional work, link it to assignment argument and referencing. Many PGT health students are experienced practitioners for whom the focus is on articulating tacit expertise in academic terms.
reviewNotes: Terminology varies (evidence-based medicine, practice, nursing, healthcare); the topic uses evidence-based practice as the umbrella term.

guidance.summary: Reflective writing in health draws on Schön's (1983) account of reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action and is usually scaffolded with models such as Gibbs's (1988) cycle or Rolfe et al.'s (2001) What? So what? Now what? framework. Models help, but used mechanically they produce long descriptions and superficial analysis. Ryan (2011) proposes making the language of deeper reflection explicit: shifts from past-tense report to present-tense analysis that draws on theory, and to future-oriented action. Programmes differ in the model they require and in the use of first person, so check the brief and use local exemplars.

activities.title: Weighing the stages
learnerActions: Read two anonymised reflections on the same type of placement incident, one high-scoring and one low-scoring
Highlight the description, feelings, analysis and action-plan stages in different colours and estimate the proportion of each
Identify the language that marks analysis (because, this may reflect, according to) and the sources each writer uses
Revise the low-scoring reflection's analysis paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: Marks are earned in analysis and action planning, and analysis uses different language and draws on literature.
activities.rationale: Comparing high- and low-rated texts makes the valued features visible, and attention to tense and evidential language follows Ryan's social semiotic approach.

activities.title: From feeling to explanation
learnerActions: Write three sentences describing how you felt during a challenging communication on placement or in study
For each feeling, write a 'so what' sentence that explains it using a concept, standard or piece of research
Add a 'now what' sentence for each that names a specific, observable change
activities.intendedInsight: In professional reflection, feelings are data to be explained, not the conclusion.
activities.rationale: The What? So what? Now what? structure directs the writer from experience to meaning and action, which is where professional reflection is assessed.

difficulties.pattern: Following the model stage by stage with equal weight, so that description and feelings take most of the word count.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reflections that are long on narrative and short on analysis, with feedback such as 'too descriptive'.
difficulties.response: Set word budgets for each stage and use exemplars to show typical proportions. Do not ban description; it should be selective and serve the analysis.

difficulties.pattern: Writing about personal mistakes feels unsafe or inappropriate, so I present everything as positive.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reflections with no acknowledged difficulty or learning, or with vague statements of improvement.
difficulties.response: Discuss the professional purpose of reflection and the programme's guidance on what is safe to disclose. Model professional, measured self-evaluation, and respect that comfort with self-disclosure varies with prior schooling and individual experience.

difficulties.pattern: Identifying patients, staff or wards, or describing them in judgemental terms.
difficulties.revealedBy: Names, dates, locations or evaluative descriptions of colleagues in draft reflections.
difficulties.response: Teach anonymisation conventions and professional language explicitly, with reference to the programme's confidentiality policy.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a 200-word reflection on a short scenario, using the model their programme requires.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Brief anonymised description, analysis that explains the event with reference to a concept or standard, and a specific action plan, with appropriate tense shifts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Follows the stages but analysis is limited to personal feelings, or the action plan is generic.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Narrative account of the event with an evaluative conclusion and no analysis.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional health pathways, introduce reflection as a genre and its tense and stance patterns. UG nursing, midwifery and allied health students write reflections from the first placement onwards. PGT practitioners may need help to make reflection analytical and to link it to advanced practice literature.
reviewNotes: Use of particular reflective models (Gibbs, Driscoll, Johns, Rolfe et al.) varies by programme; the topic is model-neutral.

guidance.summary: Case presentations and care plans are genres in which selection and order of information support clinical reasoning. Lingard et al. (2003) found that students' case presentations were shaped by tensions between school expectations (completeness, display of knowledge) and workplace expectations (relevance to the clinical problem), so teaching should make the decision-making purpose explicit. Nesi and Gardner (2012) identify the case study as a genre family in which health students apply professional knowledge to a specific case. Formats differ between professions and institutions, so local templates and exemplars are essential.

activities.title: What matters for this patient?
learnerActions: Receive a full set of notes on a fictional patient
Decide which details are essential, useful or irrelevant for a presentation focused on the presenting problem
Give a two-minute presentation in the conventional order and receive feedback on selection and ordering
activities.intendedInsight: A case presentation selects information for a clinical purpose; completeness is not the goal.
activities.rationale: Selection for relevance addresses the school–workplace tension Lingard et al. describe in student case presentations.

activities.title: Linking need to intervention
learnerActions: Read a care plan with goals and interventions but no rationales
Rewrite each goal so it is specific and measurable
Add an evidence-based rationale for each intervention, citing a source, and an evaluation criterion
activities.intendedInsight: A care plan is an argument from assessed need to intervention to evaluation, and every link needs justification.
activities.rationale: Making the rationale explicit connects care planning to evidence-based practice and to the case-study genre's purpose of applying knowledge to a case.

difficulties.pattern: Including everything known about the patient to show thoroughness.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long presentations with the presenting problem buried, and feedback asking 'what is the point?'.
difficulties.response: Show model presentations with a clear clinical focus and discuss how relevance is decided. Bring in a clinical educator to explain what supervisors listen for.

difficulties.pattern: Using abbreviations from a previous hospital, country or textbook that are not used, or mean something different, locally.
difficulties.revealedBy: Abbreviations queried by assessors or ambiguous in the local context.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to check the approved abbreviation list for the placement and to expand any abbreviation that could be misread.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to order ten scrambled statements from a case presentation and to delete two that are not relevant to the presenting problem.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces the conventional order, deletes the irrelevant items and explains why.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Orders most items correctly but keeps irrelevant details or misplaces examination findings and history.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Orders the statements chronologically by when events happened, regardless of the conventional structure.

guidance.contextNotes: Medical students meet oral case presentations on clinical attachments; nursing and allied health students more often write care plans and case studies. At PGT, case studies may require more critical engagement with evidence and service context.
reviewNotes: The skeleton bundles two genres (case presentation and care plan) with different structures and professions; consider splitting.
Published case reports in journals follow specific reporting guidance not covered here.

guidance.summary: Clinical communication is taught in health programmes through consultation models such as the Calgary–Cambridge guide described by Silverman et al. (2013), which set out structures for initiating, gathering information, explaining and planning, and closing. For multilingual students, the additional challenges are pragmatic (mitigating requests to senior staff, managing face with patients) and receptive (colloquial and regional speech). Politeness theory (Brown & Levinson, 1987) gives a vocabulary for discussing these choices, and Gigerenzer et al. (2007) show that how risk is framed affects patient understanding. Structured handover formats differ by service, so learners should check which is used on their placement.

activities.title: Lay explanation with explain-back
learnerActions: Prepare an explanation of a common procedure or condition for a patient with no medical knowledge
Deliver it in a role-play and ask the 'patient' to explain it back
Note where the explanation broke down and revise the wording, chunking information and replacing jargon
activities.intendedInsight: Checking understanding by asking the patient to explain back reveals misunderstandings that 'Do you understand?' hides.
activities.rationale: Explaining and checking understanding are core components of consultation models used in health education, and role-play allows safe rehearsal.

activities.title: Escalating to a senior colleague
learnerActions: Read a scenario in which a patient's condition is deteriorating
Plan a concise call to a senior colleague using the structured format used locally (situation, background, assessment, recommendation or similar)
Role-play the call and discuss how directness and politeness were balanced
activities.intendedInsight: In escalation, clarity and directness serve patient safety, and a structured format supports them.
activities.rationale: Politeness theory helps learners see that the degree of mitigation suitable in an academic request may be inappropriate when patient safety is at stake.

difficulties.pattern: Mitigating too much when raising concerns with senior staff ('I'm sorry to bother you, maybe if you have time…').
difficulties.revealedBy: Escalations in role-play or on placement where the concern and the request are unclear.
difficulties.response: Contrast the purposes of academic requests and clinical escalation, and practise a structured format that puts the concern first. Do not suggest that deference itself is wrong; show when the situation calls for directness.

difficulties.pattern: Not recognising colloquial or regional expressions for symptoms or body parts.
difficulties.revealedBy: Students who report that patients are hard to understand, or who misrecord symptoms.
difficulties.response: Build a class glossary from placement experiences, practise clarification questions, and use recordings of varied accents. Encourage asking rather than guessing.

difficulties.pattern: Using technical terms with patients because they are the precise terms learned in class.
difficulties.revealedBy: Role-plays in which patients look confused and the student does not notice.
difficulties.response: Practise translating terms into lay language and back. Make explain-back routine.

diagnostic.task: In a three-minute role-play, the learner must gather a brief history from a patient who uses one colloquial symptom description and then explain the next step.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses open then closed questions, clarifies the colloquial expression, acknowledges the patient's concern and checks understanding by asking for an explanation back.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gathers information but ignores the expression or relies on 'Do you understand?'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Asks only closed questions, uses jargon and does not check understanding.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional health pathways should introduce the basic interactional patterns before placements begin. UG students need support around first placements. International PGT practitioners may be clinically experienced but new to the communication norms and accents of the local health system.
reviewNotes: Clinical communication assessment (for example OSCE stations) is governed by professional programmes; EAP support should be coordinated with clinical skills staff.
Handover formats such as SBAR or ISBAR vary by service; no specific source is cited for them here.

guidance.summary: Appraisal tools structure the questions a reader asks about validity, results and applicability (Greenhalgh, 2019), but students often reproduce checklist answers rather than producing a judgement. Teaching should focus on turning appraisal findings into calibrated evaluative prose and on the vocabulary of bias and generalisability. For systematic reviews, the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021) specifies what to report, and teaching it as a reporting standard, not a template for argument, helps PGT and PGR writers.

activities.title: From checklist to judgement
learnerActions: Complete a design-appropriate appraisal checklist for a short study
Group the checklist answers into strengths and weaknesses and rank them by their likely effect on the results
Write a paragraph that gives an overall judgement and explains how the main weakness limits applicability
activities.intendedInsight: A checklist identifies issues; the written appraisal must weigh them and reach a conclusion.
activities.rationale: Structured appraisal is standard in health education, and converting it into weighed prose targets the evaluative step that markers reward.

activities.title: Reporting a review transparently
learnerActions: Read the methods section of a published systematic review alongside the PRISMA checklist
Mark which items are reported, where and how
Draft the search and selection paragraph for your own review and a flow diagram, then exchange with a peer to check against the checklist
activities.intendedInsight: Review methods are reported so that a reader could replicate the search and selection.
activities.rationale: Using the reporting guideline as an analytical lens on an exemplar connects genre analysis to the standard the discipline applies.

difficulties.pattern: Listing every limitation with equal weight, so that every study appears flawed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Appraisals that conclude a study is 'unreliable' without weighing the importance of each weakness.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to rank limitations by their likely effect and to state what the study can still support. Avoid praising long lists of weaknesses as criticality.

difficulties.pattern: Treating the appraisal tool's headings as the essay structure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments organised as question-and-answer under checklist headings where an argued critique was required.
difficulties.response: Show exemplars of continuous appraisal writing and discuss how the brief signals the expected format.

diagnostic.task: Give a methods and results summary of a small study and ask for a 150-word appraisal paragraph ending with a recommendation about applicability.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the key validity issue, explains its likely effect, acknowledges strengths and gives a calibrated judgement about applying the findings.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies weaknesses but lists them without weighing, or concludes without linking to them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the study without evaluation.

guidance.contextNotes: UG health students meet appraisal in research modules, often with one study. PGT students write appraisals and literature-based dissertations, sometimes as structured reviews. PGR students write full systematic reviews and need detailed control of reporting standards and risk-of-bias language.
reviewNotes: The skeleton combines appraisal of single studies with systematic review reporting; these are distinct genres at different levels.
CASP and other appraisal tools are named as examples but not cited; tool choice varies by programme.

guidance.summary: Stylistics, as introduced by Short (1996), offers a systematic, linguistically grounded way into close reading: noticing foregrounding through deviation and parallelism, and connecting linguistic features to interpretation. This makes tacit literary-critical practice explicit, which benefits learners new to the discipline. Learners' own metalinguistic awareness from other languages can support the noticing stage. Because interpretation is valued over correct answers in humanities fields (Becher & Trowler, 2001), teaching should reward plausible, evidenced readings rather than a single meaning.

activities.title: Notice, then interpret
learnerActions: Read a short passage and list everything you notice about its language, without interpreting yet
Group your observations into patterns (repetitions, contrasts, shifts)
Choose one pattern and write a paragraph explaining what it contributes to meaning, quoting individual words
activities.intendedInsight: Interpretation is stronger when it grows from systematic noticing of patterns rather than from a general impression.
activities.rationale: Stylistic approaches make the observation-to-interpretation process explicit through foregrounding, deviation and parallelism.

activities.title: Two readings of one detail
learnerActions: Examine an ambiguous word or image in a passage
In pairs, develop two different interpretations, each supported by textual evidence
Write a paragraph that presents both and argues for one
activities.intendedInsight: Humanities interpretation is argued, not discovered, and alternatives strengthen an argument when addressed.
activities.rationale: Working with competing readings reflects the interpretive, plural character of knowledge in soft-pure disciplines.

difficulties.pattern: Retelling what happens in the passage instead of analysing how it is written.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that paraphrase plot or content, with feedback such as 'too much narrative' or 'analyse, don't describe'.
difficulties.response: Contrast summary and analysis using the same passage, and require each sentence to refer to a specific word or formal feature.

difficulties.pattern: Spotting devices and naming them ('This is a metaphor') without explaining their effect.
difficulties.revealedBy: Analyses that list techniques without linking them to meaning.
difficulties.response: Use a three-part frame (feature, effect, significance) and ask 'so what?' after each observation. Do not reward terminology for its own sake.

difficulties.pattern: There must be one correct interpretation, and I need to find what the teacher thinks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to commit to an interpretation, or reliance on study guides.
difficulties.response: Discuss how interpretations are judged by evidence and plausibility, show published critics disagreeing, and value evidenced original readings.

diagnostic.task: Give a short poem or prose passage and ask for one analytical paragraph in 15 minutes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies a pattern, analyses specific words with brief quotations and connects features to an interpretation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names devices accurately but explains their effect only in general terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the content without analysis of language or form.

guidance.contextNotes: On foundation and pre-sessional humanities pathways, build the noticing-to-interpretation sequence with short texts. UG students need support with depth and with using critical terminology. PGT students are expected to connect close reading with theory and critical debate.
reviewNotes: Close reading practices differ between literary studies, history and philosophy; examples here lean towards literary studies.

guidance.summary: Wineburg (1991) found that historians reading documents routinely used heuristics that novices did not: sourcing (attending to author and provenance), contextualisation and corroboration across documents. Coffin (2006) shows how student historical writing develops from recounting to explaining and arguing, which depends on treating sources as evidence to be interpreted rather than as records. Teaching should model these heuristics with authentic sources and make citation conventions for primary materials explicit, in consultation with the department and archivists.

activities.title: Source before content
learnerActions: Before reading a document's content, note its author, date, type, intended audience and purpose
Predict how these might shape what it says
Read the document and write two sentences on what it can and cannot reliably tell you about a stated question
activities.intendedInsight: The value of a source depends on who produced it and why, in relation to the question asked.
activities.rationale: Sourcing is a heuristic Wineburg observed in historians but not in novices, so modelling it targets a key difference in expertise.

activities.title: Corroboration table
learnerActions: Read three short sources on the same event
Tabulate where they agree, disagree and are silent
Write a paragraph explaining the discrepancies with reference to each source's origin and purpose
activities.intendedInsight: Discrepancies between sources are themselves evidence about perspective and context.
activities.rationale: Corroboration and explanation of difference move student writing from recount towards historical argument.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a document as a neutral record of what happened.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that quote primary sources as fact without considering authorship or purpose.
difficulties.response: Make sourcing a routine first step and ask for a reliability comment whenever a primary source is used.

difficulties.pattern: Not knowing how to cite archives, manuscripts or translated sources.
difficulties.revealedBy: Incomplete or inconsistent citations for primary materials, missing repository or translation details.
difficulties.response: Provide models in the required style and liaise with the department and library on local expectations.

diagnostic.task: Give a primary source with a clear author and purpose and ask the learner to write a short commentary on its usefulness for a stated question.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Sources and contextualises the document, notes what it reveals and what it obscures, and suggests what other sources would corroborate it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Summarises content and mentions the author but does not link authorship to reliability.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the document as factual narrative.

guidance.contextNotes: UG history and related students meet primary sources in seminars and coursework. PGT dissertations often involve archival work for the first time. PGR researchers need detailed control of archival citation, transcription and translation conventions and of research ethics for archives.
reviewNotes: Wineburg's study compared historians with high-school students; the heuristics are widely applied in university teaching but the study did not test university learners.

guidance.summary: Coffin (2006) describes a developmental path in historical writing from recount genres, through explanation, to argument genres (exposition, discussion and challenge), in which evaluation and engagement with other views become central. Martin and White's (2005) engagement system gives a vocabulary for how writers position their interpretations among others, and Hyland (2004) shows that humanities and social science writers use more explicit evaluation of sources and authorial presence than scientists. Teaching should help learners formulate arguable interpretive theses, build paragraphs around claims, and position themselves in the critical conversation.

activities.title: Is it arguable?
learnerActions: Sort a set of thesis statements into summary, fact and interpretation
Rewrite the summary and fact statements as interpretive claims
Test each claim by writing the opposing claim and judging whether a reasonable reader could hold it
activities.intendedInsight: An interpretive thesis is a claim that could be disputed and must be argued.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing recount and record from argument targets the developmental shift Coffin identifies in historical and other humanities writing.

activities.title: Entering the critical conversation
learnerActions: Read two short critical views on a text or historical question
Highlight the language each writer uses to agree, concede, counter or extend
Write a paragraph positioning your interpretation in relation to both critics
activities.intendedInsight: Interpretation is made persuasive by engaging other readings explicitly.
activities.rationale: The engagement system describes how writers open and close dialogic space, giving learners concrete resources for positioning.

difficulties.pattern: Writing a thesis that summarises the text or restates a fact.
difficulties.revealedBy: Introductions with descriptive theses and essays that follow the order of the text.
difficulties.response: Practise converting summaries into claims and organising paragraphs by argument rather than by chronology of the text.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding disagreement with published critics because they are authorities.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that report critics' views approvingly without positioning the writer's own reading.
difficulties.response: Model respectful disagreement and extension, and show exemplars where students challenge critics. Present this as a disciplinary expectation, not a rejection of respect for authority.

difficulties.pattern: Using long quotations that substitute for analysis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Block quotations followed by brief comment.
difficulties.response: Require short, embedded quotations and analysis that is longer than the quotation.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write an interpretive thesis and one supporting paragraph on a short set text or source.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Arguable thesis, claim-led paragraph with brief analysed quotations, reference to an alternative reading.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Interpretive thesis but paragraph drifts into summary or uses quotation without analysis.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Descriptive thesis and summary paragraph.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional humanities pathways, focus on the move from summary to interpretation. UG students need support with claim-led paragraphs and quotation. PGT and PGR writers must position original interpretations within critical or historiographical debates over long texts.
reviewNotes: Conventions differ markedly between literary studies, history and other humanities fields; exemplars should come from the learner's discipline.

guidance.summary: Philosophy essays are organised around reconstructing and assessing arguments, and Walton (2006) provides tools for identifying argument structure and the critical questions that test it. Hyland (2001, 2004) found that writers in philosophy and other soft fields use self-mention far more than those in the sciences, which supports teaching first-person signposting as a disciplinary convention rather than discouraging it. Teaching should emphasise charitable reconstruction, targeted objections and clear distinctions, and should use departmental guidance and model essays.

activities.title: Standard form
learnerActions: Read a short passage presenting a philosophical argument
Rewrite it as numbered premises and a conclusion, adding any unstated premise needed for validity
Compare reconstructions with a partner and decide which is more faithful and charitable
activities.intendedInsight: Reconstruction is an interpretive act that should present the argument at its strongest.
activities.rationale: Identifying premises, conclusions and implicit assumptions is central to argument analysis as Walton describes it.

activities.title: Objection and reply
learnerActions: Choose one premise from a reconstructed argument
Write an objection using a counterexample or thought experiment
Write the strongest reply the original author could give, then a paragraph assessing whether the reply succeeds, using first-person signposting
activities.intendedInsight: Philosophical argument progresses through targeted objections and replies, with the writer's moves made explicit.
activities.rationale: Objection–reply practice reflects the dialectical structure of philosophy essays, and first-person signposting is a documented feature of philosophical writing.

difficulties.pattern: Summarising what philosophers said, in historical order, without evaluating the arguments.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays that resemble history-of-ideas surveys with little argument assessment.
difficulties.response: Show model essays where exposition serves evaluation, and limit exposition to what the argument needs.

difficulties.pattern: Objecting to a conclusion because I disagree with it, without identifying which premise fails.
difficulties.revealedBy: Objections that state an opposing view rather than targeting the argument's structure.
difficulties.response: Teach validity and soundness explicitly and require every objection to name the premise or inference it targets.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding 'I' because I was taught it is not academic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Convoluted impersonal constructions where a philosopher would write 'I will argue'.
difficulties.response: Show evidence of self-mention in philosophy and the department's guidance. Present 'never use I' as a myth, while noting that conventions vary.

diagnostic.task: Give a short argumentative passage and ask the learner to reconstruct it in standard form and raise one objection.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Faithful, valid reconstruction with any implicit premise made explicit, and an objection targeting a specific premise with a counterexample.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reasonable reconstruction but the objection is a general disagreement.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summary of the passage without premise–conclusion structure.

guidance.contextNotes: UG philosophy students meet these conventions from the first year, often with departmental style guides. PGT students may come from other disciplines and need explicit induction. PGR researchers need to sustain argument across long texts with careful signposting.
reviewNotes: Philosophical writing conventions differ between analytic and continental traditions; this topic reflects mainly analytic practice common in UK departments.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) shows that features often criticised as obscure in legal English, such as complex qualifications in legislative sentences, serve the drafter's aim of precision and all-inclusiveness. Mertz (2007) describes legal education as a linguistic reorientation in which students learn to read texts for legal categories and authority rather than for moral or narrative meaning. Teaching should therefore explain the functions of legal features, distinguish what learners need to recognise from what they should produce, and emphasise that legal terms belong to a specific legal system.

activities.title: Same word, different law
learnerActions: Collect five words from a case you are reading that have both everyday and legal meanings
Write the everyday meaning and the legal meaning side by side, using a legal dictionary to check
Write one sentence in your own words using each word in its legal sense
activities.intendedInsight: Many difficult legal words look familiar, and the familiar meaning can lead to a wrong reading.
activities.rationale: Reading for legal rather than everyday meaning is the reorientation Mertz describes as central to legal education.

activities.title: Why is it written like this?
learnerActions: Read a short statutory provision and a plain-language version of it
Identify what the original says that the plain version leaves out or makes less precise
Discuss which features of the original you should recognise when reading and which you should avoid in your own analytical writing
activities.intendedInsight: Legal drafting features serve precision and inclusiveness, but student analysis is expected to be clear rather than imitative.
activities.rationale: Bhatia's analysis of legislative writing shows how its complexity follows from its purpose, which helps learners read it without imitating it.

difficulties.pattern: Translating legal terms through a bilingual dictionary or assuming they mean what the closest term means in the legal system I studied.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misuse of concepts such as consideration, equity or trust, which have no direct equivalent in many civil-law systems.
difficulties.response: Treat legal terms as system-specific concepts. Use an English legal dictionary and the cases that define them, and note differences from the learner's home legal system as a comparative resource.

difficulties.pattern: Imitating archaic drafting in my essays (hereinafter, the said party, aforementioned) because it sounds legal.
difficulties.revealedBy: Student essays and problem answers with drafting formulas that markers mark as unclear or inappropriate.
difficulties.response: Distinguish reading legal drafting from writing legal analysis, and show model answers in clear academic prose.

diagnostic.task: Give six sentences from judgments and statutes, each with a highlighted word, and ask the learner to explain the meaning of each in context.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives the legal meaning for all items and explains how the everyday sense would mislead for at least two.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises some legal senses but defaults to everyday meanings for less familiar words.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives everyday meanings throughout.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional law pathways, focus on recognition and on frequently confused legal senses. UG students need terminology tied to core modules. LLM students often know legal concepts in their own system well, so comparative discussion is valuable, alongside explicit warning about false equivalents.
reviewNotes: The topic assumes common-law, primarily English, legal English; programmes in other jurisdictions should adapt examples.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) describes legal cases as a genre with recognisable moves (identifying the case, establishing the facts, arguing the case, pronouncing judgment), which gives learners a map for reading. Twining and Miers (2010) treat reading cases and extracting the ratio as an interpretive skill, noting that the ratio is not stated in the judgment and that its formulation can be contested. Mertz (2007) shows that law students learn to read cases for legal authority and procedure rather than for the human story. Teaching should model the process of briefing, practise it with real judgments, and discuss competing formulations of the ratio.

activities.title: Map the judgment
learnerActions: Skim a short judgment and mark where the facts, procedural history, arguments, reasoning and decision appear
Highlight the sentences that state the legal principle the decision depends on
Compare the headnote with your reading and note anything the headnote simplifies
activities.intendedInsight: Judgments have a recognisable structure, and the headnote is a guide to them, not a substitute.
activities.rationale: Genre awareness of the moves in a legal case supports strategic reading of long judgments.

activities.title: How wide is the ratio?
learnerActions: Write the ratio of a case in one sentence
Compare formulations across the group, from very narrow (tied to the exact facts) to very broad
Discuss which formulation the material facts justify, and identify one obiter statement and why it is not binding
activities.intendedInsight: Formulating the ratio is an interpretive act, and its level of generality matters for later cases.
activities.rationale: Twining and Miers present the ratio as something readers construct from the judgment, which group comparison makes visible.

difficulties.pattern: Reading the judgment from start to finish and summarising everything, or relying only on the headnote.
difficulties.revealedBy: Case briefs that retell the facts at length, or that reproduce headnote wording without the reasoning.
difficulties.response: Teach strategic reading with the case structure and set a strict length for briefs. Explain that the headnote is not authority.

difficulties.pattern: Treating everything a senior judge says as binding law.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays and problem answers that cite obiter remarks as if they were the ratio, or dissenting judgments as authority.
difficulties.response: Practise separating ratio, obiter and dissent, and explain precedential weight with the court hierarchy.

diagnostic.task: Give a 500-word extract from a judgment and ask the learner to identify the issue, the decision, the ratio in one sentence and any obiter remark.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the issue as a legal question, formulates a ratio grounded in material facts and correctly identifies obiter remarks.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies issue and decision but gives a ratio that restates the outcome or confuses it with obiter.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the facts without identifying the legal principle.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional law pathways, use short, accessible judgments. First-year LLB students need briefing practice early, coordinated with their legal method modules. LLM students from civil-law systems may be used to codes and academic doctrine as primary sources and need explicit work on precedent.
reviewNotes: Mertz's study concerns US law schools; its relevance to UK legal education is by analogy.
The four-move description of legal cases is attributed to Bhatia (1993) from memory; the move labels should be checked against the book before publication.

guidance.summary: Problem questions test the application of legal rules to facts, which Twining and Miers (2010) treat as a core interpretive skill of legal method. Scaffolds such as IRAC help novices organise answers, but they are contested: lecturers vary in whether they recommend them, and applied mechanically they lead to rule-stating with little application. Teaching should use IRAC-type structures as a starting point, foreground application to facts and the handling of ambiguity, and follow the conventions of the specific law school, including OSCOLA footnoting (Goudkamp, 2026).

activities.title: Issue spotting
learnerActions: Read a problem scenario and underline every fact that may have legal significance
Group the facts into legal issues and decide the order in which to address them
Compare your list with a lecturer's model issue list and discuss any issues you missed
activities.intendedInsight: Each significant fact is usually there for a reason, and missing an issue costs more than imperfect expression.
activities.rationale: Issue identification is the first step of applying rules to facts and a common source of lost marks.

activities.title: Apply, don't recite
learnerActions: Read two answers to the same issue: one that states the law at length and one that applies it closely to the facts
Highlight sentences that mention the specific facts of the scenario
Rewrite a rule-heavy paragraph so that at least half of it applies the rule to the facts, using analogy with or distinction from a decided case
activities.intendedInsight: Marks are earned mainly in application: connecting the rule to these facts through comparison with decided cases.
activities.rationale: Comparing answers makes the balance between rule statement and application visible, addressing a known weakness of mechanical IRAC use.

difficulties.pattern: Writing everything I know about the area of law and then giving a one-line conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that resemble essays on the topic, with little reference to the parties or facts.
difficulties.response: Show the marking criteria for application and require each paragraph to mention a fact from the scenario. Avoid presenting IRAC as a formula to fill.

difficulties.pattern: Giving certain conclusions ('X will definitely win') or refusing to conclude because the law is uncertain.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions that overstate certainty or leave the client without advice.
difficulties.response: Teach language for calibrated advice (is likely to, has a strong argument that, may be able to) and show how lawyers advise despite uncertainty.

difficulties.pattern: Inventing facts to resolve ambiguity in the scenario.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that assume facts not stated, such as what a party intended.
difficulties.response: Model conditional analysis that addresses each possibility (if X intended…, if, however,…). Explain that examiners include ambiguity on purpose.

diagnostic.task: Give a short problem scenario raising one main issue and one ambiguous fact, and ask for a 250-word answer advising one party.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the issue, gives the rule with authority, applies it closely with an analogy or distinction, addresses the ambiguous fact conditionally and concludes with calibrated advice.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the issue and rule correctly but applies them thinly or ignores the ambiguity.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Discusses the area of law generally without applying it or advising the party.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, introduce the genre with short scenarios. First-year LLB students need support as they meet problem questions in exams and coursework. LLM students may not have met problem questions in their prior legal education, which often used other assessment forms.
reviewNotes: Critiques of IRAC are widespread among legal educators, but no source in the bibliography documents them; a legal-education source on IRAC should be added if verified.
Some UK law schools discourage IRAC labels, others teach it explicitly; check local practice.

guidance.summary: Bhatia (1993) analyses legislative provisions as sentences in which qualifications are inserted at points of potential ambiguity to make the provision precise and all-inclusive, which explains much of their reading difficulty. Twining and Miers (2010) treat statutory interpretation as reasoning about rules and their purposes, not only as the parsing of text. Teaching should combine structural parsing (main rule, conditions, exceptions, definitions) with awareness of how courts approach interpretation.

activities.title: Statute to flowchart
learnerActions: Read a statutory subsection and identify the main rule
Mark each condition, exception and cross-reference
Draw a flowchart or decision tree showing when the rule applies, then test it against two short fact scenarios
activities.intendedInsight: A long provision becomes manageable when its rule, conditions and exceptions are separated.
activities.rationale: Bhatia's account of qualificational insertion explains where the complexity lies, and visualising the structure supports accurate reading.

activities.title: Same words, different readings
learnerActions: Read a short provision with a known interpretive problem
In groups, argue for a literal reading and for a purposive reading
Write one paragraph explaining which reading you prefer and why, referring to the purpose of the Act
activities.intendedInsight: Reading legislation involves interpretive choices that courts justify by reference to the text and its purpose.
activities.rationale: Treating interpretation as reasoning about rules follows Twining and Miers' approach to statutory interpretation.

difficulties.pattern: Reading 'and' and 'or' between conditions loosely, so that cumulative conditions become alternatives or vice versa.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that apply a provision when only one of several cumulative conditions is met.
difficulties.response: Practise marking conjunctions in provisions and converting them into lists and flowcharts. Slow, structural reading is expected here.

difficulties.pattern: Ignoring the definitions section and reading defined terms in their ordinary sense.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misapplication of provisions in which a term has a specific statutory meaning.
difficulties.response: Make checking the interpretation section a routine step and show cases where a definition changed the outcome.

diagnostic.task: Give a 70-word statutory provision with two cumulative conditions and an exception, plus two short scenarios. Ask whether the provision applies in each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Applies the provision correctly to both scenarios and explains the conditions and the exception.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the main rule but misreads a condition or the exception.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Answers from general fairness without reference to the provision's structure.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, use short provisions to build structural reading. UG students meet statutes in public, criminal and contract law. LLM students need efficient navigation of long Acts and secondary legislation, and may compare common-law statutory interpretation with civil-law code interpretation.

guidance.summary: Legal essays combine accurate exposition of the law with argument about it, and students often over-describe cases at the expense of evaluation. Mertz (2007) shows that legal reading attends to the authority and procedural position of texts, which in essays becomes a hierarchy of sources and reporting verbs with legal meanings. OSCOLA (Goudkamp, 2026) specifies footnote referencing for UK law schools. Teaching should use the school's exemplars, model how case discussion is subordinated to a thesis, and make legal reporting conventions explicit.

activities.title: From case list to argument
learnerActions: Read a paragraph that summarises three cases in turn
Decide what claim the three cases could support together
Rewrite the paragraph with the claim first and each case used as evidence, with OSCOLA footnotes
activities.intendedInsight: Cases are evidence for an argument about the law, not the content of the essay in themselves.
activities.rationale: Reordering source-by-source paragraphs into claim-led ones targets the most common weakness in legal essays.

activities.title: Who said what, with what authority?
learnerActions: Collect reporting verbs from a model essay and sort them by who they report (court, judge, counsel, commentator, Law Commission)
Discuss why 'held' is reserved for the court's decision and what 'observed' or 'suggested' signals
Correct the reporting verbs in a short student paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: In legal writing, reporting verbs signal legal authority as well as stance.
activities.rationale: Making legal reporting conventions explicit connects general reporting-verb knowledge to the authority structure Mertz describes.

difficulties.pattern: Describing the facts of every case at length.
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays in which case narratives dominate, with feedback such as 'too descriptive' or 'what is your argument?'.
difficulties.response: Limit facts to those needed for the point and require a claim sentence at the start of each paragraph. Do not ban case facts; select them.

difficulties.pattern: Citing textbooks for propositions of law instead of the primary authority.
difficulties.revealedBy: Footnotes to textbooks where the marker expects a case or statute.
difficulties.response: Explain the hierarchy of authority and the role of secondary sources in legal argument, and practise tracing a textbook statement to its primary source.

diagnostic.task: Give a 'To what extent…' legal essay question and ask the learner for a thesis statement and one body paragraph with footnotes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Takes a clear position, uses cases as evidence for a claim, evaluates against a criterion and footnotes correctly in OSCOLA.
diagnostic.partialResponse: States a position but the paragraph describes cases with little evaluation, or references are inconsistent.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the law without a position and without legal referencing.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional law pathways, contrast legal essays with general argumentative essays. UG students need early support with OSCOLA and with using cases as evidence. LLM essays expect more theoretical and comparative depth, and LLM students may bring different conventions for referencing and for the role of academic doctrine.
reviewNotes: Some institutions use OSCOLA variants or other legal citation guides; check local requirements.

guidance.summary: Halliday's analysis in Halliday and Martin (1993) treats the features that make scientific English hard (interlocking definitions, technical taxonomies, lexical density, grammatical metaphor) as functional resources that evolved to build and argue about technical knowledge. Teaching therefore aims at making these resources visible and usable, not at simplifying them away: learners practise unpacking nominalised sentences into congruent clauses and repacking them, and map the taxonomies that terms belong to. Lemke (1990) adds that science is learned by talking and writing its semantic relations, so learners should rehearse the relations between terms, not only the terms.

activities.title: Unpack and repack
learnerActions: Take a dense sentence from a course textbook and underline every noun that names a process or quality
Rewrite the sentence as a series of short clauses with human or physical agents and verbs
Compare versions with a partner and decide what the original version gains (flow from the previous sentence, compactness, a nameable concept) and what it loses (agency, explicit causal relation)
Repack a different explained sequence into one sentence using a process noun as the subject
activities.intendedInsight: Nominalisation lets science turn a process into a thing that can be measured, classified and used as the starting point of the next claim, at the cost of hiding who did what.
activities.rationale: Halliday's account of grammatical metaphor explains both the function and the reading difficulty of nominalised scientific prose, and moving between congruent and metaphorical wordings makes the resource visible.

activities.title: Taxonomy mapping
learnerActions: List the technical terms introduced in one section of a textbook chapter
Arrange them in a diagram showing classification (types of) and composition (parts of) relations
Write two definition sentences that use the diagram's superordinate terms (for example a covalent bond is a type of chemical bond in which…)
Check the diagram against a glossary or a subject lecturer's explanation
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific terms are organised into systems, and knowing a term includes knowing its place in the system.
activities.rationale: Halliday and Martin and Lemke both describe technical taxonomies as central to how science organises meaning, and making them explicit gives learners a structure for vocabulary learning.

difficulties.pattern: Scientific texts are hard just because the vocabulary is difficult. If I learn the words I will understand.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who can gloss every word in a sentence still misread which process caused which, or cannot say what a nominalised subject refers back to.
difficulties.response: Show that difficulty often lies in grammar: process nouns, long nominal groups and implicit causal links. Practise unpacking. Do not simply pre-teach word lists and assume comprehension follows.

difficulties.pattern: Using everyday meanings of words that are technical in the discipline (writing that a force 'has power' or a result is 'significant' meaning important).
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that are grammatical but scientifically wrong, often flagged by subject markers as conceptual errors.
difficulties.response: Contrast everyday and technical uses side by side and ask learners to collect pairs from their own reading. Involve subject staff in checking which distinctions matter most in the module.

difficulties.pattern: Packing every sentence with nominalisations to sound scientific, producing writing that hides agents and causal steps.
difficulties.revealedBy: Student drafts with strings of abstract nouns that markers comment on as unclear or wordy.
difficulties.response: Present nominalisation as a choice with costs. Ask learners to justify each nominalisation by what it does for text flow and to unpack those that do nothing. Avoid presenting density as a target in itself.

diagnostic.task: Give a 40–60-word textbook extract with two nominalisations and one sub-technical term. Ask the learner to explain it orally in plain terms and then identify which word has a special scientific meaning.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Recovers the underlying processes and agents, keeps the causal direction, and identifies the sub-technical term and its scientific sense.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Paraphrases the general topic but blurs the causal relation or replaces a technical term with an everyday synonym.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Translates word by word or restates the sentence unchanged, unable to say what happens to what.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation, work from textbooks and practical classes, with a strong focus on taxonomies and unpacking. On pre-sessional science pathways, use subject texts to build awareness of the register. In-sessionally, connect the work to the student's actual module reading and to markers' comments about clarity. At PGT, discuss when compressed prose is expected in research writing and when it becomes unreadable.

guidance.summary: Sydney School genre research distinguishes several explanation genres (sequential, causal, factorial, consequential, conditional) with predictable stages: identifying the phenomenon, then an explanation sequence (Martin & Rose, 2008). Explicit teaching of these stages through deconstruction, joint construction and independent construction is a central proposal of the Reading to Learn pedagogy (Rose & Martin, 2012). Gardner and Nesi (2013) also identify Explanation as a distinct genre family in university student writing, particularly in science and technology disciplines.

activities.title: Which kind of explanation?
learnerActions: Sort six short textbook explanations into sequential, factorial and consequential types
Highlight the identifying statement and the language that links each step or factor
Choose an explanation type for each of three exam questions from your subject and justify the choice
activities.intendedInsight: The question asked determines the shape of the explanation, and each shape has its own linking language.
activities.rationale: Identifying the staging and purpose of explanation genres before writing them follows the deconstruction phase of the Sydney School teaching–learning cycle.

activities.title: Joint construction with a diagram
learnerActions: Start from a labelled diagram of a process from your module, such as a cycle or a circuit
Build an explanation together with the teacher, deciding the order of steps and the causal verb for each link
Write a second explanation independently from a different diagram and compare it with a model
activities.intendedInsight: Diagrams show stages but not reasons; the written explanation must add the causal links.
activities.rationale: Joint construction scaffolds the move from understanding a model text to producing one, and diagram-to-text work reflects how science presents explanations multimodally.

difficulties.pattern: Narrating what happened in one experiment ('First we heated the water, then…') when the question asks for a general explanation of a mechanism.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers in past tense with personal agents and specific quantities, where the marker expected present-tense general statements.
difficulties.response: Contrast a recount of a practical with an explanation of the phenomenon it demonstrates. Show the shift to present simple and to generic participants.

difficulties.pattern: Listing steps or factors joined by 'and' or 'then' without saying how one causes the next.
difficulties.revealedBy: Explanations that read as sequences of true statements but lose marks for 'no explanation of why'.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to label each link with the causal relation (causes, enables, prevents) and to choose a verb or conjunction for it. Do not correct only surface linking words; check the logic of each step with subject knowledge.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a familiar phenomenon from their subject in writing in about 120 words, with an optional sketch.
diagnostic.strongResponse: States the phenomenon, then orders the steps or factors, links each causally, uses technical terms accurately and stays general.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Covers the right content but with weak or missing causal links, or slips into a recount of a particular case.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the topic or gives a definition without any explanation sequence.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional science pathways this is a core genre for exams and short answers. In UG in-sessional work, link it to exam answers and to the discussion sections of lab reports, where theoretical explanation of results is expected.
reviewNotes: The theoretical explanation type in the scope note is not a separate Sydney School category; it is interpreted here as applying a model or law to a specific case.

guidance.summary: Procedural and specification texts are judged by whether they can be carried out or tested without ambiguity, so teaching should focus on precision, sequencing and the conventional meanings of modal verbs in the relevant community. Trimble (1985) describes instructions and rhetorical functions such as description of process and of physical structure as central to scientific and technical English. Gardner and Nesi (2013) identify Design Specification as a genre family in student writing. Conventions for modal verbs and formatting vary across standards bodies, companies and departments, so learners should check the local standard or template with subject staff.

activities.title: Follow it exactly
learnerActions: Write a protocol for a simple procedure (for example preparing a 0.1 M solution or setting up a piece of software)
Exchange protocols with a partner, who follows the steps literally and records every point where they had to guess
Revise the protocol to remove each guess, adding quantities, conditions, timings or warnings
activities.intendedInsight: A protocol is only as good as the questions it leaves unanswered for the person following it.
activities.rationale: Literal execution makes ambiguity visible to the writer, a form of reader feedback that matches the genre's purpose.

activities.title: Testable requirements
learnerActions: Read a short design brief and underline every vague expression (fast, user-friendly, approximately)
Rewrite each as a single requirement with a measurable criterion and unit
Assign each requirement a modal verb according to the convention your department or the relevant standard uses, and justify the choice
activities.intendedInsight: Specification language turns intentions into statements that can be passed or failed.
activities.rationale: Converting vague briefs into verifiable statements targets the core function of the design specification genre and the precise use of units and quantities.

difficulties.pattern: Writing protocols in the past passive ('The solution was heated') because that is how lab-report methods are written.
difficulties.revealedBy: Protocols or SOPs that read as reports of what was done rather than instructions to follow.
difficulties.response: Place a protocol and the corresponding lab-report method side by side and discuss how purpose and reader change mood, tense and voice.

difficulties.pattern: Using should, must and will interchangeably in requirements, or using 'shall' and 'should' in their everyday senses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Specifications in which the obligation level of each requirement is unclear; this is more likely where the learner's first language marks obligation differently or with fewer distinctions.
difficulties.response: Teach the convention used by the relevant standard or department explicitly as a convention, and have learners audit their own specifications for consistency.

difficulties.pattern: Omitting units, conditions or tolerances because they seem obvious to the writer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Quantities without units, temperatures without duration, or settings without the equipment model.
difficulties.response: Use a checklist for quantity, unit, condition, duration and equipment for each step. Peer testing is more effective than teacher correction alone here.

diagnostic.task: Give a five-step protocol containing one missing unit, one warning placed after the hazardous step and one step that combines two actions. Ask the learner to edit it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Fixes all three problems and explains how each would affect a person following the protocol.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices the missing unit but not the misplaced warning or the compound step.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Edits only grammar or style and leaves the procedural problems untouched.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation students mostly read protocols in practical classes, so focus there on reading instructions accurately. UG and PGT engineering and computing students write specifications in design projects. PGR students may write SOPs, method statements or protocols for ethics and safety approval, where institutional templates apply.
reviewNotes: The modal-verb convention (shall/must for mandatory, should for recommended, may for optional) varies between standards bodies and organisations; it is presented as a convention to check locally, not as a universal rule.

guidance.summary: Experimental vocabulary is a site where language and conceptual understanding are inseparable: confusion between accuracy and precision, or between significance and importance, often signals a misunderstanding of method. Parkinson's (2017) analysis of the student laboratory report shows how aims, methods and discussions rest on this vocabulary, and Hyland's (1998) work on scientific hedging shows that expert writers tie certainty to the strength of experimental evidence. Teaching should pair language work with simple experimental scenarios and, where possible, with lab demonstrators' feedback.

activities.title: Variable detective
learnerActions: Read three short experiment descriptions from your subject
Identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables and the control condition in each
Write a hypothesis and a prediction for each, and compare formulations with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: A hypothesis states a relationship between named variables, and a prediction says what should be observed if it holds.
activities.rationale: Working from authentic experimental designs ties the vocabulary to the concepts it encodes, as in the aims and methods stages of student lab reports.

activities.title: Error and uncertainty clinic
learnerActions: Examine sets of repeated measurements that are precise but inaccurate, accurate but imprecise, and both
Label each set and write one sentence describing it with appropriate vocabulary
Rewrite three overclaiming result statements so that they state the value with its uncertainty and make a claim the data can support
activities.intendedInsight: Accuracy, precision and uncertainty are different properties, and claims should not exceed what the measurements show.
activities.rationale: Connecting the language of uncertainty to claim strength reflects how scientific writers calibrate certainty to evidence, and to statistical guidance against equating significance with importance.

difficulties.pattern: Using 'error' to mean a mistake by the experimenter, and listing 'human error' as the main limitation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion sections that blame 'human error' without naming a source of random or systematic error or its effect on the result.
difficulties.response: Teach the scientific sense of error as uncertainty, and ask learners to name a specific source, classify it and suggest how it could be reduced. Agree with lab staff what level of error analysis is expected.

difficulties.pattern: Writing hypotheses as questions or as vague expectations ('Temperature will affect the reaction').
difficulties.revealedBy: Hypotheses that do not state the direction or nature of the relationship and so cannot be tested.
difficulties.response: Model the move from question to directional hypothesis to measurable prediction. Note that some fields and some lab reports do not require formal hypotheses, so check the brief.

diagnostic.task: Give a results table from a simple experiment, with repeats, and ask the learner to write two sentences: one reporting the result with uncertainty, one evaluating the reliability of the data.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reports a mean with an appropriate uncertainty and significant figures, and evaluates spread and possible systematic error using the correct terms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reports the mean but without uncertainty, or uses accuracy and precision interchangeably.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies values without interpretation or attributes all variation to 'human error'.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and on pre-sessional science pathways, link this to practical classes and simple data. In UG in-sessional work, align it with lab reports and demonstrator feedback. At PGT the focus shifts to statistical language and uncertainty in project work, where num.interpreting-statistics becomes more relevant.

guidance.summary: Software documentation is a family of genres defined by readers with different tasks: a newcomer deciding whether to use a project, a developer calling an API, a maintainer reading code months later. Robillard's (2009) survey of developers found inadequate documentation, especially missing examples and explanations of intent, to be a major obstacle to learning APIs, which supports teaching documentation around reader tasks rather than templates. Conventions differ between languages, frameworks and teams, so learners should analyse documentation from well-maintained projects in their own ecosystem and check module requirements.

activities.title: README rescue
learnerActions: Compare two READMEs from open-source projects in your language, one that you find easy to use and one that you do not
List the sections each contains and what questions a newcomer can or cannot answer from each
Rewrite the README of one of your own projects so that a classmate can install and run it, then test it with that classmate
activities.intendedInsight: A README is judged by whether a newcomer can get started without asking the author.
activities.rationale: Analysing authentic exemplars and then testing with a real reader applies genre analysis to a professional genre whose success criteria are practical.

activities.title: Why, not what
learnerActions: Read a short code file with a mix of comments
Classify each comment as restating the code, explaining intent, warning of a constraint or out of date
Rewrite or delete comments accordingly and write one docstring with parameters, return value, errors and an example
